opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the distinction is less about any single benchmark and more about a few qualities that current models only partially have.

The first is **generality in the true sense**. Today's models are remarkably broad, since they can write code, summarize papers, and chat about philosophy. But much of that breadth comes from having seen a huge amount of human-produced data. A real AGI would handle genuinely novel situations, ones that don't resemble anything in its training distribution, as robustly as a capable person does. Current systems can still fail in surprisingly brittle ways when you step slightly outside familiar territory.

The second is **continual learning**. A person who starts a new job is mediocre the first week and much better six months later, because they accumulate context, learn from mistakes, and build intuition. Most current models are essentially frozen after training. They can use what's in their context window, but they don't really *grow* from experience in a durable way. I'd consider this one of the biggest missing pieces.

The third is **long-horizon autonomy and reliability**. Models are getting good at tasks that take minutes, and increasingly hours. But AGI would mean you could hand it an open-ended goal that takes weeks, like running a research project or building a product, and it would plan, recover from failures, ask the right questions, and know when it's stuck. The key word is reliability. Being right 90% of the time on each step falls apart over a hundred steps.

The fourth is something like **grounded understanding and self-knowledge**: knowing what it knows and what it doesn't, and having a model of the world that's consistent rather than locally plausible.

So my practical test would be economic and experiential rather than academic: can it do most of the cognitive work a competent professional does, in a new domain, learning on the job, without someone constantly holding its hand? We're clearly closer than we were a few years ago, but I don't think we're there yet. Honestly, the last stretch, especially reliability and continual learning, may turn out to be the hardest part.

fable-5.1.text:
This is a question I think about a lot, and honestly my answer has changed over the past couple of years.

The simplest test I use now is this: can the system learn something it didn't know when it left training, and can it carry that learning forward? Current models are extraordinary at compressing what humanity has already written down. But when you give them a genuinely new problem, something not in the data, they are mostly recombining. They don't go to sleep and wake up having understood it better. Every conversation starts from the same frozen weights. A human researcher who fails at a problem on Monday is a different person by Friday. The model is not.

The second thing I look at is the gap between performance and understanding. Today's models can score higher than most humans on an exam and then make an error a child wouldn't make, in the same minute. That jaggedness tells you something. Real general intelligence isn't just high average capability, it's a kind of consistency. The capabilities hang together. When a person understands something deeply, it shows up in how they handle edge cases, how they notice when a question is badly posed, how they say "wait, that doesn't make sense." Models are getting better at this, but it's still fragile.

The third marker, and maybe the most practical one, is autonomy over long horizons. Can it pursue a goal for weeks, notice when its own plan is failing, change strategy, and manage its own attention without a human steering every few steps? Right now we've gone from models that can work for seconds to models that can work for hours. That's enormous progress. But there's a very long way between hours and the kind of sustained, self-correcting agency we take for granted in a competent adult.

I'd add one caveat. I'm suspicious of definitions of AGI that keep moving so that the thing we have never qualifies. Five years ago, if you'd shown someone today's models, they'd have said "that's AGI." So I try to hold two thoughts at once: these systems are already general in a way that would have seemed like science fiction, and they're still missing continual learning, robust understanding, and long-horizon autonomy. When those three arrive together, I don't think we'll be debating the definition anymore. It'll be obvious.

astra-6.text:
For me, the key distinction is how well a system handles something genuinely new. Current AI models can be remarkably capable, but that capability is uneven. A model might solve a difficult coding problem and then miss a basic assumption in the next question.

I’d expect real AGI to learn unfamiliar tasks, transfer what it learns across domains, and adjust when its approach fails—without people having to guide every step. It should also recognize when it lacks information and seek out what it needs.

So I wouldn’t judge it by one impressive conversation or benchmark score. I’d look for reliable performance across unfamiliar situations, over time. Can it figure out what matters, learn from mistakes, and keep making progress? That’s a much stronger test than whether it sounds intelligent.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish them by how well they handle unfamiliar situations. Current models can be remarkably capable, but they’re uneven: they may solve a difficult problem and then fail at something simple, especially when the task requires sustained planning or checking their own assumptions.

For me, real AGI would be able to learn a new task, transfer what it knows across domains, and work toward a goal reliably with limited guidance. It would also recognize when it doesn’t know something and seek the information it needs.

So I wouldn’t judge it by one impressive conversation or benchmark score. I’d look for broad, consistent performance on genuinely new problems.
